sections.h: What a skimmer does that filters do not
sections.body:
A protein skimmer pulls dissolved organics out of saltwater before they break down into nitrate. Air and water are mixed into a fine foam in the reaction chamber, the organics stick to the bubbles, and the foam rises into the collection cup where you throw it away. A mechanical filter only catches particles. A skimmer removes the dissolved material that filters cannot, which is why most reef keepers treat one as basic equipment.

It is for marine and reef tanks only. It does nothing useful in a freshwater planted tank.

sections.h: Sizing and the first two weeks
sections.body: This unit is a needle-wheel skimmer with a pump rated for tanks up to about 400 litres. Rated capacity assumes a normally stocked tank, so a heavily stocked or heavily fed reef wants a skimmer rated well above its water volume. When a skimmer is new it overflows or produces thin, watery skimmate for the first week or two. That is normal and is caused by manufacturing residue and a dry reaction chamber. Run it with the cup off and keep the water level steady until the bubbles settle.

The collection cup height sets how wet or dry the skimmate is. Raise the cup for drier, darker skimmate that needs emptying less often. Lower it and you pull more liquid through, which is fine for a new tank. Skimmers are sensitive to water level, to oils and to additives. Add new foods, coral dips and supplements slowly and watch how the foam responds. Clean the cup and the neck regularly, because a layer of scum stops bubbles from rising.

faqs.q: Can I use a protein skimmer in a freshwater tank?
faqs.a: No. A skimmer needs the surface tension and salt content of seawater to make stable foam. In freshwater it produces little or nothing. For freshwater, use mechanical and biological filtration plus regular water changes.

faqs.q: How often should I empty and clean it?
faqs.a: Empty the cup when it is full, which might be every few days to weekly depending on feeding and stocking. Rinse the cup and neck with fresh water each time, and clean the pump and needle wheel every few months so the output stays steady.

sections.h: A small filter for small jobs
sections.body: This is a slim internal filter for nano tanks and fry grow-out tubs. It sits fully under the water on a suction mount, the flow is adjustable, and it is quiet enough for a desk or a bedroom. It is the kind of filter that suits a shrimp cube, a betta tank or a temporary rearing tank where a hang-on-back would be too big and a sponge filter would need an air pump.

Shrimp, bettas and fry are all harmed by strong flow. Turn the flow down until the surface ripples gently and plant leaves move a little, and aim the outlet along the glass or at the back wall rather than across the open tank. Position it so it is covered by water but not buried in plants, and check the intake periodically for debris, which cuts the flow before it cuts the noise.

Rinse the sponge or cartridge in a bucket of old tank water every few weeks when the flow starts to drop. Never use tap water, which kills the bacteria. If you are rearing fry, a fine sponge over the intake stops them being drawn in. Replace the media only when it falls apart, and when you do, keep part of the old media in place so the bacteria carry over.

faqs.q: Is it safe for shrimp and fry?
faqs.a: Use the lowest flow that keeps the water moving, and cover the intake with a piece of fine sponge so small animals cannot be sucked in. Always check the suction cups on a new filter in the first days.

faqs.q: Can it be the only filter in a nano tank?
faqs.a: For a lightly stocked nano tank, yes, together with regular water changes and live plants. The sponge also carries the bacteria that process ammonia, so look after it.

sections.body: The backdrop comes in three scenes: rock cave, rainforest and coral reef. Pick the one that matches your hardscape or where the fish come from. Rock cave goes with dark stone and cichlids, rainforest suits planted tanks and tropical community fish, and the reef scene is a good fit for brightly coloured fish. The print is double-sided, so you can flip it when you rescape.

Measure the height and length of the rear glass before you cut. Trim the sheet to size with scissors, then tape it to the outside of the back glass or slide it between the glass and the stand so there is no gap where light can leak. A covered back panel also reduces reflections from the room and blocks the view of cables and equipment behind the tank.

A plain glass back means a fish sees its own reflection and the room behind it. In territorial species that can cause constant flashing and glass-surfing. A solid backdrop gives them a visual boundary and tends to calm them. Dark, deep scenes also make colours stand out, so lighting looks richer without any extra power.

faqs.q: Does it go inside or outside the tank?
faqs.a: It goes on the outside of the rear glass, taped in place or held between the glass and a stand. Keeping it dry is the simplest way to stop it peeling or colour running.

faqs.q: Can I use it with a bare-bottom or planted tank?
faqs.a: Yes. It suits both. For a planted tank, choose the rainforest scene, which blends with foliage and keeps the focus on the plants rather than competing with them.

sections.body: Both versions have two independent outlets. The 3 W pump suits a single smaller setup, for example a sponge filter and a small air stone on one nano tank. The 5 W pump holds pressure across both lines at once, so it is the better pick when you run two tanks, a deeper tank or longer tubing. A pump that is too weak will bubble gently at the surface and stop doing anything useful once the airline is long.

Fit a [check valve](/product/bubble-counter-check-valve-set) on each airline below the water line. If the power goes out the pump stops and water can siphon back along the tube, flood the pump and run onto the floor. A one-way valve takes a minute to fit and removes that risk. Place the pump above water level where possible, on a firm, flat surface so the rubber feet can do their job.

The pump drives [sponge filters](/product/bio-sponge-filter-4-pack), air stones, bubble walls and other airline accessories. Use a splitter or one of the two outlets for each device and adjust each outlet so there is a steady, quiet flow of bubbles rather than a violent boil. Keep the pump clean and replace the diaphragm when it starts to get noisy or weaker.

faqs.q: Is the pump quiet enough for a bedroom?
faqs.a: Pumps vary in noise, and a firm mounting surface and soft feet help most. A hum that travels through the stand is usually vibration rather than air noise, so a foam pad under the pump often fixes it.

faqs.q: Can I run it 24 hours a day?
faqs.a: Yes. Air pumps are designed to run continuously. Keep the intake clear of dust and replace the diaphragm and filter pad when airflow drops.

sections.body: Plants need macronutrients (nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium) and trace elements (iron and others) in balance. This liquid carries both. Dosed weekly it is the backbone of a planted-tank routine for stems, rosettes and carpeting plants, whether or not you inject CO2. The aim is not maximum growth. It is a steady supply so plants keep outcompeting algae.

sections.h: Matching dose to light and CO2
sections.body: Light, CO2 and nutrients limit each other. A tank on strong light with CO2 uses fertiliser quickly and needs full dosing. A tank with low light and no CO2 needs much less and can fall into algae if over-dosed. Start at half the recommended dose and watch the plants for a few weeks. New leaves that come in pale or pinholed point to too little. Green spot or hair algae after raising the dose points to too much or too much light.

The pump bottle makes it a five-second job once a week. Dose after a water change so the nutrient level resets each week, and keep it to the same day so you can trace cause and effect if algae appears. Heavy root feeders such as sword plants also benefit from [root tabs](/product/root-fertilizer-tabs-40) pushed into the substrate, which feed the roots directly.

faqs.q: Is it safe for shrimp and fish?
faqs.a: Used at the labelled dose it is intended for planted tanks with fish and shrimp. Copper-sensitive shrimp are the animals to watch with any fertiliser, so start lower and read the label for details.

faqs.q: Can I use it in a tank with no CO2?
faqs.a: Yes. Use a lighter dose, since slow-growing plants use fewer nutrients. Match the dose to the plants rather than to the bottle.

sections.body: Nitrifying bacteria convert ammonia to nitrite and nitrite to nitrate. A new tank has too few of them, which is why it needs a cycle before fish are safe in it. A dose from this bottle seeds the colony, shortens the wait and gives you a backup when the filter has been bruised by medication or a deep clean.

For maintenance, use 10 ml per 50 litres. For a new or stressed tank, double it. Shake the bottle, dose into the tank, and keep the filter running. Treat tap water with a dechlorinator first, because chlorine and chloramine kill the bacteria you have just added. A 300 ml bottle is enough for one full cycle plus months of top-ups on a mid-size tank.

Add an ammonia source, either a small amount of fish food or pure ammonia, dose the bacteria and test with [test strips](/product/test-strips-8-in-1-100-count) every few days. The cycle is finished when ammonia and nitrite both read zero within a day of adding more ammonia, and nitrate appears. Bottled bacteria speed things up but do not guarantee a finished cycle, so test before you add fish, and add them gradually.

faqs.q: How long does it take to cycle a tank with this?
faqs.a: It varies with temperature, water and what you start with. Expect days to a few weeks rather than hours. Trust the test results, not the calendar.

faqs.q: Do I still need to test the water after dosing?
faqs.a: Yes. Bottled bacteria shorten the cycle but do not remove the need to check ammonia and nitrite. Keep testing until both read zero and nitrate appears, then stock gradually.

sections.body: This kit is the front end of a pressurised CO2 system: a dual-gauge regulator with a built-in solenoid, a 304 stainless inline atomiser and a glass drop checker with a 4 dKH reference solution. The cylinder is not included. Buy that locally: it is cheaper than shipping one, and it can be refilled nearby. Check that the regulator's thread matches the cylinder you plan to buy.

The solenoid is the reason to choose this regulator. Plug it into a mains timer and CO2 turns on and off by itself. Plants only use CO2 while the lights are on, and at night they release it. A common schedule starts CO2 about an hour before the lights come on, so the level has built up, and stops it an hour before they go off. Leaving CO2 running overnight is a common cause of fish gasping in the morning.

Fill the glass drop checker with the reference solution and hang it in the tank where it can see circulating water. Blue means too little CO2. Green means about right. Yellow means too much. The colour lags the tank by an hour or two, so adjust the bubble rate a little at a time and check it the next day, not in the same sitting. Replace the solution every month or two so the reading stays accurate.

The atomiser dissolves CO2 into the water as a fine mist and works best in the water line of a canister filter. Make sure the tubing is the right size for your filter hoses. Start with a slow bubble count and raise it over several days while you watch both the plants and the livestock. If you want a lower-cost way to try CO2 first, the [DIY CO2 kit](/product/diy-co2-generator-kit-2l) is a smaller commitment.

faqs.q: Do I need a cylinder with this?
faqs.a: Yes. The bundle includes the regulator, solenoid, atomiser and drop checker, but not the cylinder. You will need a CO2 cylinder, filled at a local gas supplier or aquarium shop.

faqs.q: Why does the drop checker take so long to change colour?
faqs.a: The solution inside the glass has to reach equilibrium with the CO2 in the tank, which takes an hour or more. Change the bubble rate in small steps and wait before judging.

sections.body: This is the bigger sibling in the Aurora range, built for larger planted tanks and paludariums. It comes in 92 cm, 112 cm and 132 cm lengths, and the extendable brackets fit rims from 90 to 120 cm. Measure the outside length of your rim and choose the closest bar that is not longer than the tank. A bar that is too short for the tank leaves the ends of the scape in shadow, so two short bars spaced evenly can be better than one that is too small.

The bar is full-spectrum and RGB, set from a Bluetooth app, with a colour rendering index of 90.6. You can dim it, shift the colour balance toward the plants or the fish, and adjust the schedule from your phone. Keep a consistent daily schedule for the plants rather than changing the mix constantly, since erratic lighting is a common cause of algae.

The body is aluminium with silicone sealing and is listed as IP68. Even so, we recommend mounting it above the water and away from splashes, and keeping the plug end dry. It is available with AU, US, UK and EU plugs, so check the plug type on the option you choose. The manufacturer does not publish wattage for each length separately, and we do not publish a PAR figure because none has been supplied.

faqs.q: Which plug will I get?
faqs.a: Plug options are AU, US, UK and EU. Choose the one for your country, and check it matches before you order.

faqs.q: Will it light a tank deeper than 50 cm?
faqs.a: A deep tank loses light at the bottom, so expect weaker growth on the floor. Pair it with plants that tolerate lower light at depth, or raise the plants on hardscape closer to the light.

sections.body: 300 gallons per hour is about 1,135 litres per hour. That is the pump's rated flow with no resistance. Add height, tubing and a filter and the real flow is lower, so pick a pump with some margin. It suits medium tanks, a sump return, a refill pump or a small pond loop. In a planted aquascape this is a lot of flow, so plan to spread it with a spray bar or turn it down.

The pump has built-in filtration, so it traps debris as it moves water. That works as a first stage on a sump or as a simple filter on a medium tank. The impeller can be reached without tools, which makes cleaning quick. Check the intake before you buy for shrimp or fry. Fine animals can be drawn into any strong pump, so cover the intake with a fine sponge.

Keep the motor fully submerged unless you are running it inline. Use a pre-filter sponge on the intake if the water is dirty, and make sure the outlet tubing is not kinked, which cuts the flow and strains the motor. Clean the impeller every few months, and never run it dry.

faqs.q: Is it quiet enough for a living room?
faqs.a: The motor is sealed and quiet, but any submerged pump sends vibration into the tank. Put it on a rubber pad or suction feet for the quietest run.

faqs.q: Can I use it as a return pump in a sump?
faqs.a: Yes, as long as the head height and tubing do not take the flow far below what you need. Check the pump's flow at your required height before you commit.

sections.body: These pebbles absorb light and release it slowly, so they glow in the dark after the tank light goes out. They charge under your tank light during the day and glow for a few hours after the lights turn off, fading as the energy is used. The effect is subtle, a soft accent for pathways and borders, not a replacement for lighting.

Use them in small amounts along a path, around a rock base or on the front edge of a tank. They look best on dark substrate, where the glow is clear, and when used sparingly. Too many look artificial. Rinse before adding them and check for any chips or flaking.
Like any decoration they will collect algae and film over time. Brush them with a soft brush during water changes. If the glow fades over months, move them to a spot that gets more direct light.

faqs.q: How long do they glow after the light goes off?
faqs.a: The glow fades over a few hours, brightest in the first part of the night. Longer charge under brighter light gives a stronger glow.

faqs.q: Can I use them in a shrimp tank?
faqs.a: They are decorative stones. As with anything new, rinse them well and watch for flaking or changes in the water before adding to a sensitive shrimp tank.

sections.h: The last layer in the filter
sections.body: Foam catches the large debris and floss catches what it lets through. A white floss pad is the polishing stage that makes water look clear rather than almost clear. Place it last in the chain, after the sponge and [bio media](/product/ceramic-bio-rings-filter-media), so it only has to catch the fine specks and does not clog on coarse waste.

Cut it with scissors to the size of a hang-on-back tray, canister basket, sump baffle or internal filter. Make it slightly larger than the space so it fills the cross-section and water cannot go around it. Fluff the edge a little so there is a loose layer rather than a compressed one.

Swirl the pad in a bucket of tank water once a week and squeeze gently. Replace it when it stays grey after rinsing and the flow has dropped. Floss is cheap and is meant to be replaced more often than the media behind it. Never rinse it under the tap if it has become your main biological surface.

faqs.q: How often should I change filter floss?
faqs.a: Rinse weekly and replace when it stays discoloured or the flow drops. In a heavily stocked tank that may be every couple of weeks. In a lightly stocked planted tank it can last much longer.

faqs.q: Will it fit my filter?
faqs.a: It is cut to size, so yes for most trays and baskets. Measure your media chamber and cut a pad slightly larger.

sections.body: Bloodworms are rich in protein, and almost every fish goes for them. Use these cubes a few times a week alongside a quality flake or pellet, not instead of it. A fish fed only bloodworms misses vitamins and fibre and can become constipated or bloated. Variety is what keeps fish in colour and in condition.

Press a cube against the glass just below the waterline, and it releases slowly as the fish pick at it. For smaller fish, break a cube apart, or soak it in a little tank water for a minute before dropping it in. Freeze-dried food swells when it gets wet, so soaking first reduces the chance of a fish swallowing a dry piece that expands in the gut.

Bettas, tetras, cichlids, discus, many marine fish, turtles and frogs all take bloodworms. Bottom-dwellers may need the cube to sink, and shy fish do better when you feed away from aggressive tank mates. Feed only what is eaten in a minute or two and remove leftovers, since uneaten food fouls the water. No freezer is needed, so keep the tub sealed and dry.

faqs.q: How many cubes should I feed at a time?
faqs.a: One small cube for a tank of small fish, and break it up if needed. Feed only what is eaten in a minute or two.

faqs.q: How should I store them?
faqs.a: Keep the tub tightly closed in a cool, dry place. Moisture spoils freeze-dried food.
